_comment: Russian folk tales cut from Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), Project Gutenberg #16981. All passages paraphrase.

title.en: The Silver Saucer and the Transparent Apple

region.zh: 俄羅斯村莊（象徵性定位於羅斯托夫）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Tale of the Silver Saucer and the Transparent Apple'

summary.en: A kind stepdaughter finds a silver saucer and a transparent apple in a beggar's pack; rolled on the saucer, the apple shows any city she wishes — until it shows her the drowned daughter of the tsar, and only her kind answer to the drowning woman can end the tale.
summary.zh: 善良繼女自乞丐行囊中得銀碟與晶蘋果；蘋果置碟上滾動，可照見心中所願之城——直至映出溺水而亡的沙皇之女；唯她善意作答，方能終結亡靈之囑。

passages.text: A poor widow's little daughter gives her bread to a beggar at the gate, and the beggar leaves in the pack a silver saucer and a transparent apple. Rolled on the saucer, the apple shows any city she asks for — and the stepmother's own daughter, greedy to see more, asks for the one city no one may look on: the city of the dead tsar's daughter, drowned in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Silver Saucer and the Transparent Apple'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the crystal city of the dead the daughter of the tsar sits in a white chamber, and her voice comes through the apple: 'Who loves me more than all the world?' The kind girl answers, 'I do, poor drowned daughter of the tsar,' and takes up the saucer — but the voice is not done. She runs weeping to the river and tells the tsar; they drag the river, find the princess with a silver moon on her breast, and lay her in the palace in a glass coffin among flowers.

Then the kind girl is sent for, and the drowned tsar's daughter rises in her coffin and gives her the silver saucer and the transparent apple as her own — for the kind girl had been the only one who ever answered her. The stepmother and her lazy daughter are shut out of the house for ever, and the tsar makes the kind girl his daughter; and some say the drowned princess took her dulcimer and swam back into the Volkhov to look for the little shepherd who had loved her.

title.en: Sadko and the Sea-King: The Gusli That Stopped the Sea
title.zh: 薩德科與海王：令海止息的古斯里琴

region.zh: 諾夫哥羅德與伊爾門湖（象徵性定位）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Sadko'

summary.en: The poor gusli-player Sadko plays so beautifully on the shore of Lake Ilmen that the Sea-King rises to thank him; taught how to win gold at the merchants' feast, Sadko becomes the richest trader in Novgorod — until the sea demands him, and he plays the king to sleep among the daughters of the sea.
summary.zh: 貧苦琴師薩德科於伊爾門湖畔奏古斯里琴，樂聲之美令海王升水面致謝；習得商宴贏金之法，遂為諾夫哥羅德首富——直至大海索其人；他在海王眾女間奏樂催眠。

sensitivity.note: Novgorod bylina as retold for children.

passages.text: Poor Sadko sits twelve days on the shore of Lake Ilmen without a bite, and at last, because he has nothing else, he plays his gusli. The water of the lake stirs, and the Sea-King himself rises out of the waves to thank him: 'You have played so well that you have made the sea move when it did not wish to move — now the sea is calm again, and you shall be paid for your music.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Sadko'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He teaches Sadko how to win a wager from the merchants of Novgorod — 'buy every fish with golden fins in the market, whatever the price' — and Sadko becomes the richest man in the city, buys ships, and sails the seas trading. But the Sea-King has not forgotten him: at sea a storm rises that no sacrifice can calm, and the lot falls to Sadko to go down into the water to the Sea-King, playing his gusli all the while.

Down in the crystal palace Sadko plays for the daughters of the sea; when the Sea-King rises to dance, the storms above wreck ships, until St. Nicholas sends word that Sadko should break his gusli — for a landman cannot live under the sea. He breaks the strings, wakes on the shore of the Volkhov, and builds the church of St. Nicholas that still stands by the market in Novgorod.

title.en: Frost: The Red Nose Who Cracks the Trees

region.en: Russian winter forest (symbolic pin at Suzdal)
region.zh: 俄羅斯冬日森林（象徵性定位於蘇茲達爾）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Frost'

summary.en: Sent to freeze in the forest by a stepmother, the little stepdaughter is found by Frost — red-nosed, cracking the branches above her — who comes down lower and lower with his bitter words; her courteous answers make him cloak her in furs instead, while the stepmother's own daughter, rude to the cold, is frozen where she sits.
summary.zh: 繼母遣繼女凍死林中；紅鼻的嚴寒老人在樹上咔咔作響、步步逼近；她彬彬有禮的回答竟令他為她裹上皮裘——而繼母親女出言無禮，就地凍斃。

passages.text: The stepmother sends the old man into the winter forest to leave his daughter; the girl sits under a tree with her poor coat worn through, and Frost the red-nosed winter-god comes down crackling from branch to branch, freezing everything within reach. 'Are you cold, little maid?' 'No, thank you, kind Frost — I am warm.' Each time he comes lower and crackles louder, and each time she answers courteously, though her hands are benumbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Frost'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Frost has never been answered kindly in all his winters; he wraps her in a great fur cloak and gives her a chest of silver. At home the little dog under the table barks that she is coming home in a coach of gold; the stepmother sends her own daughter into the same forest in her best clothes to earn the same — and the rude girl answers Frost as rudely as her mother taught her, until the cold takes her voice, and she is frozen sitting, where the kind girl had been wrapped in warmth.

title.en: The Fool of the World and the Flying Ship

region.en: Village and royal palace (symbolic pin at Vladimir)
region.zh: 村莊與王宮（象徵性定位於弗拉基米爾）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fool of the World and the Flying Ship'

summary.en: The tsar promises his daughter to whoever brings him a flying ship; the fool's kindness to an old man wins him the ship, and the strange servants he feeds on the road — Hearer, Sighter, Swift-Gone, Shooter, Drinker, Eater, Frost-Blower, Wood-Thrower — win the princess against the tsar's own tests.
summary.zh: 沙皇許諾以女兒嫁獻飛船者；傻子善待老人而得船；路上以飯食所收的奇僕——善聽、善視、疾行、神射、豪飲、大食、吐寒氣、擲巨木——一一破解沙皇的刁難。

passages.text: The tsar of a great country hears that a flying ship has been seen, and offers his daughter to whoever brings it to the palace. The fool of the world, sent out with crusts while his clever brothers ride with loaves, shares his crust and his flask with an ancient old man; the old man teaches him a charm, and at a word a flying ship stands in the field, and the fool sails it toward the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fool of the World and the Flying Ship'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way he takes aboard all the strange men who beg a seat: the man who hears everything, the man who sees a hundred versts, the man who can be across the world and back with whatever you name before the water cools, the marksman, the man who drinks the sea, the man who eats the baked earth, the man who blows frost from his mouth, and the man who can carry a forest on his back.

The tsar sets the fool tasks to lose his head: to have dinner ready in a moment (the Eater swallows the kitchen and the Drinkers drain the wells), to bring running water from no well (the Hearer hears where it runs under the earth), to fetch the sword that hangs a hundred versts off (the Swift-Gone fetches it before the water cools), and to defeat the greatest archer in the empire (the Shooter beats the tsar's archer from the edge of the world). At last the fool wins the princess, and the tsar is ashamed to have tested the servants of the flying ship.

region.en: Village and forest (symbolic pin at Murom)
region.zh: 村莊與森林（象徵性定位於穆羅姆）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Cat Who Became Head-Forester'

summary.en: An old peasant sends his cat to the forest to earn a living; the cat's arched back and furious tail frighten the wolves into service, then the bear, and he ends as head-forester of all the woods with the fox as his housekeeper.
summary.zh: 老農遣貓入林自謀生計；貓弓背豎尾之怒嚇得群狼供食、棕熊上樹，終為全林總管，以狐狸為管家。

passages.text: The old peasant, unable to feed his cat, carries him to the forest: 'Live by your wits.' The cat, hungry, meets the fox, who trades on his terror — and meets the wolf, at whom he arches his back, sets all his fur on end, and says, very distinctly, 'Who are you? and how dare you?' — and the wolf, who has never seen anything sit still and dare him, brings him a lamb to keep the peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Cat Who Became Head-Forester'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then comes the bear, wanting the lamb's meat; the cat sends him up the tallest tree 'to see the hunters coming', and the fox below cries that the hunters have arrived. The bear, believing the guns are for him, jumps from the top of the tree, lands badly, and is glad to escape with his life. Thereafter the wolf brings game, the bear brings an ox, the cat lives in the fox's hole as a lord, and the forest gives him the title of head-forester, with the fox for his housekeeper and fresh meat all the days of his life.

title.en: The Little Daughter of the Snow

region.en: Russian village in winter (symbolic pin at Novgorod)
region.zh: 冬日俄羅斯村莊（象徵性定位於諾夫哥羅德）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Little Daughter of the Snow'

summary.en: An old couple make a little girl of snow, and by evening she is alive — Snegurochka, the Snow Maiden, who runs and leaps with the village children all winter; but when the sun comes, a fire is built, and the little Snow Daughter jumps over it and melts into mist, reappearing with Frost her father and Snow her mother.
summary.zh: 老夫婦以雪塑小女孩，入夜竟活——雪中少女斯涅古羅奇卡，整個冬天與村童奔跳；然春陽既至，篝火燃起，雪女躍火而過，化為輕霧，與父親嚴寒、母親白雪同去。

sensitivity.note: Snegurochka tale; living New Year icon in Russia.

passages.text: An old couple who have no children mold a little girl of snow in the courtyard, and by evening she is alive — warm, laughing, and real, 'though her hair is snow and her eyes blue as spring water'. All winter she runs and leaps with the children of the village, and no cold can touch her; but as spring comes she grows paler and thinner, and watches the others out of doors with longing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Little Daughter of the Snow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the girls of the village build a great fire to leap over, and the little Snow Daughter, who cannot refuse, runs and jumps — and melts into a little white mist that is gone. The old couple weep; but that summer the little Prince of the village dreams of her, and one winter's night a white mist drifts again over the snow and the Snow Maiden stands there once more, come from Frost her father and Snow her mother, who carried her away over the seas.

region.zh: 俄羅斯村莊（象徵性定位於特維爾）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Little Master Misery'

summary.en: A poor peasant shares his last crust with Misery, the ugly little man who squats on men's shoulders and eats their luck; in gratitude Misery leaves him, but when the peasant tries to fob Misery off on rich households and ends up selling him in a barrel to a drunkard's town, the whole city learns what the luck-eater can do.
summary.zh: 貧農以最後一塊麵包施捨蹲在人肩上吞食運氣的小苦惱；苦惱感恩離去；農夫卻試圖把苦惱轉嫁富戶，最終將其裝桶賣給酒鬼之城——全城遂識得『運氣吞食者』之能。

passages.text: Misery, the ugly little man in a torn coat, comes to squat on the shoulder of a ruined peasant and eat his luck. The peasant, having nothing else, gives Misery his last crust and half of his last drop — and Misery, who has never been treated kindly in his life, gets off the man's shoulder, and luck pours into the house: the fish fill the nets, the hens lay, the prince rides by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Little Master Misery'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the peasant grows careless, thrusts Misery out into the cold, and tries to be rid of him forever — selling him shut up in a barrel to the keeper of a tavern in a drunken town. In the barrel Misery calls himself a treasure, and the whole town is soon at ruin: every man who drinks from the barrel carries Misery home on his shoulder, luck drains out of the houses, and the drunkards' town comes to beggardom.

The peasant comes to see the mischief he has sold, opens the barrel and speaks kindly to Misery again; the little man climbs back to the shoulder of the man who shares with him — and luck returns with him, while the drunkards of the town sit in their ruined taverns, poorer than the peasant they bought their treasure from.

region.en: Russian village and forest (symbolic pin at Murom)
region.zh: 俄羅斯村莊與森林（象徵性定位於穆羅姆）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Alenoushka and Her Brother'

summary.en: Warned not to drink from the hoof-print pool, little Ivanushka drinks and becomes a kid; the witch rides into the house as Alenoushka's double, and only the lamb that bleats at the river's edge — and the white lamb that weeps so that all hear — can bring the true sister back from the bottom of the pond.
summary.zh: 小伊萬努什卡不聽勸，飲蹄印池之水而化為小羊；女巫化身冒充阿廖努什卡入主家門；唯河畔哀鳴之羔羊——白羊泣聲令眾人皆聞——方能使真姊自池底歸來。

passages.text: Alenoushka and her little brother Ivanushka walk to the fields; a cow-herd witch with evil eyes gives Alenoushka a ring to carry home her cows, and the ring works a wicked bargain. On the road the children grow thirsty, and there is a pool with a hoof-print — 'who drinks of this shall be a calf,' warns Alenoushka — and Ivanushka, minding it not, drinks and becomes a little white lamb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Alenoushka and Her Brother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Home again, the witch rides into the courtyard in the shape of Alenoushka and takes her place in the house; the true sister is thrown into the pond at the bridge with a stone round her neck, and only the lamb knows. Every day the lamb runs to the river's edge and bleats, 'Sister Alenoushka, the water is heavy on me, the stones lie cold on me!' — and the witch hears it and bids her false orders have the lamb killed.

But the little white lamb stands on the bank weeping so that all the village hears, and the truth comes out; the witch is seized, the stone taken from Alenoushka's neck, and she rises from the pond once more her own little self, to live with her brother Ivanushka, who is a boy again and never drinks from a hoof-print pool again.

title.en: The Fire-Bird, the Horse of Power, and Princess Vasilissa
title.zh: 火鳥、神駒與瓦西麗莎公主

region.en: Russian fairyland, blue sea garden (symbolic pin at Kiev)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，藍海花園（象徵性定位於基輔）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fire-Bird, the Horse of Power, and the Princess Vasilissa'

summary.en: The archer's mare bears him a foal that speaks — the Horse of Power — and with its advice he catches the Fire-Bird with golden feathers that burn like flame, is sent to fetch Princess Vasilissa from her silver boat on the blue sea, and wins all three by keeping faith with his horse.
summary.zh: 射手的老馬產下會說話的馬駒——神駒；依其計擒得羽如火焰的金色火鳥；又奉命往藍海銀舟中迎回瓦西麗莎公主——全憑對神駒守信而三願皆成。

passages.text: The archer's grey mare bears a foal that speaks, the Horse of Power: 'Sell me not, for we shall have great adventures together.' Sold and set free, the Horse of Power returns and helps the archer catch the Fire-Bird with a sack of grain scattered where it feeds — the bird with feathers of gold and eyes like living coals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'The Fire-Bird, the Horse of Power, and the Princess Vasilissa'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The tsar, wanting more, sends the archer to fetch Princess Vasilissa, who lives in a silver boat on the blue sea, rowing with golden oars among the fish. The Horse of Power leaps with him into the water; Vasilissa, half-fish and wholly beautiful, is carried off to be the tsar's bride — and the archer, who has done everything, is thrown into a pit to starve for having seen her.

But the Horse of Power comes to the pit's mouth with the water of life and the water of death, and brings the archer out; and when the tsar sends his armies to seize the princess, the Horse of Power tramples them, and the archer rides into the palace with Vasilissa, who was never meant for the tsar. The archer marries the princess of the silver boat, and the Horse of Power says at last: 'You have kept faith with me, and I with you — now you need me no more.'

title.en: Salt: The Ship to the Salt Island

region.en: Russian port and the salt seas (symbolic pin at Arkhangelsk)
region.zh: 俄羅斯港口與鹽海（象徵性定位於阿爾漢格爾斯克）

source.work: Arthur Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Salt'

summary.en: The merchant's youngest son sails for salt and is blown to an island where a devil sleeps on a casket of salt; the devil's own gold makes the voyage — and the son who was mocked for having no gift trades with a golden crown and forgives his brothers, for salt is worth more than gold.
summary.zh: 商人幼子出海尋鹽，被風吹至魔怪枕鹽箱而眠之島；借魔怪之金成此航；曾被譏『一無所有』的幼子以金冠易鹽，寬宥其兄——蓋鹽貴於金。

passages.text: The old merchant sends his sons to sea: the eldest with precious stones, the second with silver and gold cloth — and the youngest, mocked for having nothing, with a shipload of simple iron wares and a hold of salt, the cheapest thing in the port. A storm drives the little ship to an island where no man lives, and the youngest son goes ashore to see what an empty island may hold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ransome, Old Peter's Russian Tales (1916), 'Salt'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a cave sleeps a devil on a casket of salt — mountains of white salt, more than all the ships of the world could carry — and beside him lie bags of gold. The young merchant fills his hold with salt and trades in the golden bags for the salt he needs; then, when the devil wakes, he sings the devil to sleep again with his own games, and sails home by the storm that brought him.

Home, the brothers laugh that salt is worth nothing — until they understand what the youngest has: in the whole wide world salt is the one thing every kitchen must have, and the youngest son, who began with nothing, trades a golden crown's worth for every sack, and forgives the brothers who mocked him; for the merchant of the house says at last, 'Salt, my children, is worth more than gold.'
